title: Numbered list markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral (and often trailing period or bold marker) that begins an item in an enumerated list, such as '3.', '4.', '9.', or '**4.**'. It activates on the token(s) marking list-item boundaries regardless of the list's topic, appearing in contexts like step-by-step instructions, lessons learned, or numbered suggestions. It does not activate on the prose content of list items themselves, on bullet points using dashes/asterisks without numerals, or on ordinary sentences that merely contain numbers not functioning as list markers.

title: Self-help advice list items (bolded imperative tips)
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic bolded-header imperative statements from self-help/advice listicles, especially those prescribing psychological or behavioral wellness techniques like positive self-talk, mindfulness, gratitude, deep breathing, and positive body language (eye contact, posture, open gestures). It activates most strongly on the canonical, highly templated phrasing 'Practice X**: do Y' (e.g., 'Practice positive self-talk: Replace negative self-talk with positive affirmations', 'Practice mindfulness: Focus on the present moment') and related stock tips about calming techniques or confident nonverbal behavior. It does not activate on advice that is more discursive, situational, or conversational in nature (e.g., explaining why to communicate, discussing relationship dynamics, giving concrete non-wellness instructions like budgeting or packing a diaper bag), nor on plain numbered-list markers or unrelated narrative/explanatory sentences, even though these appear in the same lists.

title: Balancing counterpoint transition ('However, it's also important to consider...')
description: This latent fires on the discourse move that introduces a balancing or mitigating consideration after an initial point, typically in advice-giving contexts, using the phrase 'However, it's also important to consider/respect...'. It activates on sentences that pivot toward acknowledging another party's feelings, boundaries, or perspective (e.g., a family member's viewpoint) as a counterweight to advice already given, often as a lead-in to further elaboration or a list. It would not activate on simple contrastive statements lacking this advice-balancing framing, on 'however' used for factual contrast unrelated to interpersonal consideration, or on sentences that state a consideration without the 'it's also important to' hedging construction.

title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on standalone numeral tokens (e.g. '2.', '3.', '4.') that mark the start of an enumerated list item, typically in advice or pros/cons style responses. It activates most strongly on the bare number-plus-period token itself, regardless of what follows or what topic the list concerns. It does not activate on the prose content of list items, on first list markers like '1.' as strongly (less represented here), or on non-enumerated sentences that merely discuss reasons or perspectives without a numbered format; the distinguishing feature is the structural list-marker token, not the semantic content of advice-giving.

title: Scripted first-person assertiveness openers
description: This latent fires on short, template-like first-person utterances that begin with 'I' or a modal like 'Can'/'Would you', functioning as suggested scripts for expressing feelings, setting boundaries, or making polite requests (e.g., 'I wanted to talk to you about something that's been bothering me', 'Can we take a short break?', 'Would you mind keeping it down?'). It activates most strongly on the literal quoted phrase itself, often introduced by framing like 'You could say something like' or 'For example:', and even on bare fragments such as 'I', 'Can', or 'I'd like to' that are the grammatical start of such a scripted statement. It does NOT activate strongly on third-person or descriptive advice sentences that discuss the interpersonal situation or recommend a strategy without giving the actual first-person wording (e.g., 'Explain that you appreciate her initiative...' or 'Consider finding a compromise...'), even though these appear in the same advice-giving context.

title: Moral condemnation of someone's behavior as unacceptable/hurtful
description: This latent fires on short, evaluative sentences that explicitly label a person's behavior, words, or reaction using strongly negative moral/emotional adjectives (e.g., 'unacceptable,' 'hurtful,' 'abusive,' 'unfair,' 'dismissive,' 'manipulative'), typically in a validating, advice-column style judgment directed at 'his/her/your [relative]'s' conduct. It activates most strongly on terse declarative verdicts (often copula constructions like 'This is X and Y' or 'X's behavior was Y') that pass explicit condemnation on interpersonal conduct, especially when stacking multiple negative descriptors. It does not activate on sentences that merely describe a situation neutrally, offer advice/suggestions, express sympathy without judgment, or hedge with uncertainty ('it's possible that...', 'it's natural to...')—the latent responds specifically to direct evaluative labeling of behavior as wrong/harmful, not to surrounding empathetic or explanatory commentary.

title: Validating the user's reasonable behavior (AITA-style verdicts)
description: This latent fires on second-person statements that summarize and validate the addressee's actions or feelings as reasonable, justified, or blameless, typically in the context of an advice/verdict response (e.g., 'You were being reasonable and expressing your needs,' 'That's a reasonable request,' 'You did nothing wrong'). It activates most strongly on short, formulaic 'You + past-tense action + reasonable/valid/commendable' constructions that recap what the person did and affirm it approvingly, often as a lead-in to a not-the-asshole style judgment. It is weaker or absent on sentences that instead give advice, list pros/cons, describe third parties' actions, express empathy without direct affirmation of rightness, or explore nuance/counterarguments (e.g., 'You could have communicated more explicitly' or 'Your girlfriend might have taken it personally'), since those lack the direct restate-and-validate structure this latent tracks.

title: Formulaic empathetic acknowledgment openers
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic phrases like "I totally understand!", "I completely understand your frustration!", or "I totally get it!" that serve as a stock empathetic opener validating the reader's feelings before giving advice. It activates most strongly on the exact templated construction (subject + intensifier adverb like 'totally'/'completely' + understand/get it + optional possessive noun like concern/frustration/struggle + exclamation), typically appearing as a standalone sentence at the start of a supportive response. It activates more weakly on longer, more discursive sentences that express understanding or validation but embed it within explanatory or advisory content (e.g., "It's understandable that you...", "I'm so sorry to hear that..."), rather than using the crisp templated phrase. It would not activate on sentences offering advice, describing a situation, or making judgments (e.g., "You're not the asshole") that lack this direct first-person empathetic acknowledgment formula.

title: Formulaic supportive closing affirmations
description: This latent fires on brief, formulaic empathetic sign-off phrases that reassure the reader of their worth, strength, and right to self-care—typically starting with 'Remember,' 'You deserve,' or 'Take care of yourself,' and asserting things like being 'strong, capable, and deserving of love and respect' or 'not alone.' It activates most strongly on short, templated, almost boilerplate affirmations that could appear as the closing line of supportive/therapeutic advice text, especially ones combining a directive (remember/take care) with a validating claim (you deserve/you are worthy). It does NOT activate strongly on substantive advice-giving, situational reasoning, or judgments about who is at fault (e.g., 'you're not the asshole'), nor on analytical or list-formatted content—even when discussing similar themes of well-being or boundaries—unless phrased as this direct, formulaic second-person affirmation.

title: Age-old dilemma/debate framing
description: This latent fires on the stock exclamatory phrase used to open a response by framing an interpersonal problem as a longstanding, universal tension ('The age-old debate!', 'The age-old dilemma!', 'The eternal conundrum!'), typically as a standalone sentence introducing advice or commentary on a relationship or etiquette conflict. It activates most strongly on the bare, near-formulaic exclamation itself, and somewhat less strongly on variants that append a topic ('...of roommate etiquette!', '...about household chores!') or use synonyms like 'classic' or 'eternal conundrum'. It does not activate on general empathetic openers ('What a difficult situation!'), substantive advice sentences about communication/compromise, or age-old dilemma phrasings embedded mid-sentence rather than as the opening rhetorical exclamation.

title: Sentence-initial 'This can/will help' construction
description: This latent fires on the specific opening phrase pattern 'This can...', 'This will...', or 'This helps...' used to introduce a beneficial consequence, typically in advice-giving text about interpersonal relationships (e.g., 'This can help build trust and understanding,' 'This can help diffuse tension'). The strongest activations are on the bare template itself ('This can help', 'This can', 'This will'), essentially detecting the syntactic frame before the specific benefit is even stated, with somewhat lower but still strong activation when the phrase is completed with relationship/rapport-building outcomes (trust, connection, diffusing tension, rapport). It is triggered by the demonstrative pronoun 'This' as sentence subject followed immediately by a modal/helping verb ('can', 'will', 'helps') signaling an upcoming benefit clause, regardless of topic. It does NOT activate on sentences expressing the same advisory content through different phrasing (e.g., 'You could try...', 'It might be helpful to...', 'This might involve...') or on sentences where 'This' refers back to something as a full clause without the can/will-help construction, showing the latent is keyed to this specific syntactic template rather than the general concept of beneficial advice.

title: Direct 'what do you think?' prompt
description: This latent fires overwhelmingly on the exact, formulaic closing question 'What do you think?' (or its close variant 'What are your thoughts?'), used to invite the listener's opinion or reaction after some statement or advice. The top activations are almost entirely verbatim repetitions of this stock phrase, indicating the latent is keyed to this specific conversational closer rather than to opinion-seeking questions in general. Weaker (random) activations occur on other reflective or advice-eliciting questions ('What's important to you?', 'How do you think you'll approach this?', 'So, are you the asshole here?'), showing the latent generalizes somewhat to similar audience-directed prompts but activates most strongly on the canonical 'What do you think?' string. It would not activate on statements, advice bullet points, or questions that ask for factual/contextual information rather than soliciting the listener's opinion or reaction (e.g. 'Can you tell me more about what's going on?').

title: Numbered list markers
description: This latent fires on standalone numeral tokens (e.g., '2.', '3.', '4.') that serve as list-item markers, typically in enumerated advice or suggestion lists such as relationship or workplace guidance. It activates most strongly on the bare digit-plus-period tokens themselves, and more weakly on surrounding text within such numbered-list contexts (e.g., advice sentences embedded in a 'here are some suggestions' list). It would not activate on prose sentences lacking explicit list numbering, or on bullet points marked with symbols like '*' or '-' rather than numerals, since the core trigger is the numeric list marker pattern rather than the advice content itself.

title: Advising deference to authority/boundaries
description: This latent activates on statements that recommend accepting a decision or directive from an authority figure while respecting established limits or rules set by another party. It fires on advice-giving sentences that combine compliance ('accept the request') with respect for boundaries ('respect the boundaries'), typically in a conflict-resolution or etiquette context. It is not simply about politeness or agreement in general, but specifically about a recommended course of action that balances yielding to one party's wishes with honoring another's constraints. Sentences that merely describe a situation, express disagreement, or give advice without this dual accept-and-respect structure would not activate it.

title: List-introducing header phrase
description: This latent fires on short transitional headers that introduce an upcoming enumerated list, such as 'Here are some suggestions:', 'Here's why:', 'Here are some points to consider:', immediately followed by the start of a numbered list marker (e.g. '1.'). It activates most strongly on the exact template phrase plus the numbering start, regardless of the specific topic of the list that follows. Sentences that discuss advice-giving content itself, or that introduce a list with different phrasing embedded mid-sentence without a colon-plus-numbered-list structure, activate it weakly or not at all -- the key trigger is the formulaic header-colon-list-start pattern rather than the semantic content of the advice.

title: Listing concrete resources/services as suggestions
description: This latent fires on list items or clauses that recommend specific external resources, services, platforms, or organizations as options for accomplishing a task (e.g., 'online forums', 'VolunteerMatch', 'Uber Eats', 'local food banks', 'Coursera or Udemy'). It activates most strongly on bullet-style or enumerated suggestions naming named platforms, service categories, or institutions as actionable options in response to a need (job, money, help, learning, socializing, health). It does not activate on general advice, emotional reflections, interpersonal reasoning, or self-care/relationship guidance that lacks a concrete named resource or service being proposed as an option, nor on plain narrative or judgment statements even if list-formatted (e.g., 'NTA', numbered headers alone, or advice like 'communicate openly').

title: Reassuring normalization of universal human traits
description: This latent fires on short, affirming statements that reassure the reader by universalizing their experience or trait as normal, shared, or valuable ('everyone is unique', 'we're all human', 'nobody is perfect', 'that's a common human experience'). It activates on generic validating/comforting generalizations about human nature, individuality, imperfection, or shared struggle, typically delivered as standalone reassuring assertions rather than as advice or analysis. It also fires on bare list-numeral tokens (e.g. '2.', '3.') that likely co-occur with these enumerated reassurance lists in the training data. It does NOT activate on sentences giving specific situational advice, asking clarifying questions, describing a particular person's concrete circumstances, or offering practical/actionable steps -- even when emotionally supportive in tone, if they are tied to a specific scenario rather than a general 'we're all like this' claim.

title: AITA-style verdict query closer
description: This latent fires on the short, formulaic closing question or partial-verdict phrase used in 'Am I the Asshole' style posts and responses, most strongly on the literal tag 'AITA?' (with variants like 'So, AITA?' and 'AITAH?') and on short hedged verdict fragments like 'Not entirely.' It activates on these terse, stand-alone punctuation-marked utterances that either pose the judgment question or give a brief qualified answer to it, functioning as a discourse marker signaling 'here is the request for/delivery of a moral verdict.' It does not activate strongly on the surrounding elaborated reasoning, advice, or justification sentences (e.g., explanations of why someone is or isn't the asshole, suggestions for what to do next), even though those co-occur in the same texts and share the AITA topic -- the latent is tied to the compact query/verdict phrasing itself rather than to the substantive moral analysis.
